 Economy 'Staking Funds Drained for Ether Crash'? The Ledger Tells a Different Story, Binance Hack Fact-Check
 이단열 기자 Suwon News Updated 2026.10.31 20:44 Published 2026.10.31 20:09 Updated 2026.10.31 20:44 Three rumors verified on-chain…Hackers aren't dumping but buying, zero cash conversions The hacker is discarding assets that can be frozen and accepting losses while buying up ether that nobody can lock. /Production=Suwon Ilbo AI After the Binance hack, three rumors circulate the market: that hackers drained staking assets and converted them to ether, that they dumped it onto exchanges causing an ether crash, and that ethereum-linked ETFs got liquidated as a result. Fortunately, cryptocurrencies have an open ledger that anyone can examine—on-chain data. We verified the three rumors against the ledger.
 Rumor ① "Staking assets were drained and converted to ether" → Not true 
 The actual composition of stolen assets differs. According to analysis firm Elliptic, the $3.8 billion outflow from the Ethereum chain consists of 186 different tokens, with the largest items being stablecoin Tether (USDT) at $1.9 billion and USD Coin (USDC) at $823 million—neither ether nor staking tokens. No analyst report shows any trace of staking tokens being unstaked. Rather, Binance froze its own issued staking token wBETH, cutting off that escape route.
 Rumor ② "Dumped stolen ether to exchanges causing a crash" → Not true, the opposite actually 
 The ledger shows the opposite behavior. The hacker is buying ether, not selling it. They swapped $434 million worth of USDT for 160,451 ether on decentralized exchanges (Uniswap, 1inch), accepting losses of 12-26% below market rates. They also deposited USDT as collateral in lending protocol Aave and borrowed 19,762 ether. The reason is straightforward: stablecoins can be frozen by issuers (Tether has already locked $1.57 billion), but no one can freeze ether or bitcoin. Zero deposits to centralized exchanges; the 18,270 bitcoin secured are dormant across 19 addresses. While ether did fall to the late $2,100s shortly after the hack, this was due to broader market panic (total futures liquidations of $1.5 billion), not the hacker's selling. Ether recovered to around $2,240 by the 31st.
 Rumor ③ "ETF got liquidated" → Half true 
 No 'liquidation' occurred. The reality is net outflows from U.S. spot ethereum ETFs. On the 30th, $155.7 million flowed out in a single day, marking the fifth consecutive day of outflows and October's cumulative total of approximately $1.1 billion—the highest this year. The numbers are correct, but the causality is wrong. Most of these outflows were part of a trend predating the hack, so stating that the hack drove out ETF funds is an overstatement. There was also no price disconnect of the feared staking token (stETH). The discount rate remained at a normal 0.05%.
 So what's actually happening now? Mechanical money laundering on the TRON chain. 638 million TRX being fragmented through 546 automated transfers (96-second intervals) has allowed $38-67 million to slip past tracking. The 'non-freezable' assets remaining in the hacker's possession amount to approximately $3.2 billion. Binance CEO Richard Teng stated this attack was "not the work of a single individual," and traces of evidence-wiping and self-destruct mechanisms were found in the attack tools. Layer 2 networks Arbitrum and Optimism fully recovered their chain's stolen portions using governance authority. Binance is working to resume full withdrawals by the 1st (Korea time) and will release the Proof of Reserve (PoR) on the 2nd.
 Rumors travel fast, but ledgers don't lie. The 8 trillion won thief's next move is not dumping but a long wash cycle. It took 20 minutes to steal, but using it will take years. The battle, watched by analysis firms and law enforcement worldwide, is just beginning.
